metadata.title: Why devcontainers WILL simplify your life and other flows
metadata.description: Devcontainers help with environment uniformity for a project, we want to show how to use them, why we use them, and the time it could save. Talk about repeatble environments and other related whys
metadata.author: Webinar Maker Pro

slides.narration: Let’s start with a familiar headache: it works on my machine… but not on yours, not in CI, and not in prod... In the next ten minutes, we’re going to kill that problem with devcontainers... A devcontainer is development environment as code... It’s a simple, versioned file that defines your tools, runtimes, extensions, and dependencies, and it works the same on macOS, Windows, or Linux—locally with Docker or in the cloud with GitHub Codespaces... Here’s the mental model: you clone the repo, click Reopen in Container, and the environment builds exactly as defined... Everyone gets the same Node or Python version, the same CLI tools, and even automated setup steps like npm ci... No more tribal knowledge, no more copy‑paste install guides, and dramatically faster onboarding and context switching... By the end of this session, you’ll know how to add a minimal devcontainer to your project and spin up a clean, repeatable environment in minutes... Ready to retire “works on my machine”?... Let’s dive in.

content.title: What and Why: Dev environment as code
content.markdown:
- **Dev environment as code**
  - Declarative, versioned setup defined by the Dev Container Specification (containers.dev)
  - A devcontainer.json declares tools, runtimes, extensions, ports, and setup scripts
  - Runs consistently in VS Code Remote - Containers, GitHub Codespaces, or Dev Container CLI

- **Why it matters**
  - Uniformity across macOS/Windows/Linux → fewer “works on my machine” issues
  - Repeatability across machines, branches, and CI
  - Speed: faster onboarding and context switches with prebuilds and lifecycle hooks
  - Portability: config lives in the repo; great for teams and open source

- **Minimal example**
```json
{
  "name": "Node Dev",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu",
  "features": {
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1": { "version": "20" }
  },
  "postCreateCommand": "npm ci",
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": { "extensions": ["dbaeumer.vscode-eslint"] }
  }
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Repo[Repo with .devcontainer] --> Manifest[devcontainer.json + optional Dockerfile/Features]
  Manifest --> Image[Containerized dev image]
  Image --> Local[VS Code Remote - Containers]
  Image --> Cloud[GitHub Codespaces]
  Image --> CI[Dev Container CLI in CI]
  Local --> Same[Same tools, versions, extensions]
  Cloud --> Same
  CI --> Same
```

- **Key outcomes**
  - Hours-to-minutes onboarding; fewer env-related bugs
  - Consistent app + DB via optional docker-compose
  - Clear, auditable environment definition in version control

slides.narration:
Let’s talk about what a dev container is, and why it will simplify your life... A dev container is development environment as code... It’s a small, versioned manifest called devcontainer.json, usually in a .devcontainer folder, that declares your tools, runtimes, editor extensions, ports, and setup steps... It’s standardized by the Dev Container Specification at containers dot dev, and it runs the same whether you open the repo in VS Code with Remote Containers, in GitHub Codespaces, or via the Dev Container CLI.

Why does this matter?... First, uniformity... Everyone on the team gets the same environment across macOS, Windows, and Linux... That dramatically reduces the classic “it works on my machine” problems... Second, repeatability... The same configuration can be recreated on a new laptop, on a feature branch, or in CI, so you catch environment issues early instead of during a release... Third, speed... With prebuilt images and lifecycle hooks like postCreateCommand, onboarding goes from hours or days to minutes, and context-switching between projects no longer trashes your local toolchain... Finally, portability... Because the environment lives in the repo, open-source contributors and new hires can start building immediately without a long setup guide.

Here’s what a minimal example looks like: we point to a base image, add a Node feature set to version twenty, and run npm ci after the container is created... That’s enough to ensure everyone uses the same Node version, the same dependencies, and even the same editor extensions.

Visually, think of it as: repository, to manifest, to a containerized dev image, and then you can open it locally, in the cloud, or use it in CI, and you get the same tools and versions everywhere.

Bottom line: dev containers encode your environment, make it repeatable, and save real time... Next, we’ll walk through spinning one up and how to extend it for multi-service apps.

content.title: Live Build: From zero to a working devcontainer
content.markdown:
- Why this demo matters
  - Uniform, repeatable dev env in minutes
  - Eliminate "works on my machine" by encoding tools as code
  - Fast onboarding and context switching

- Steps we’ll do live
  1) Add .devcontainer/devcontainer.json
  2) Reopen in Container (VS Code)
  3) Run app; verify port forward

- Minimal config (Node via Feature, pinned)
```json
{
  "name": "Node Dev",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu",
  "features": {
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1": { "version": "20" }
  },
  "postCreateCommand": "npm ci",
  "forwardPorts": [3000],
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": { "extensions": ["dbaeumer.vscode-eslint"] }
  }
}
```

- App files
```json
// package.json
{
  "name": "hello-devcontainer",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "scripts": { "start": "node index.js" },
  "dependencies": { "express": "^4.19.2" }
}
```
```js
// index.js
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.get('/', (_req, res) => res.send('Hello from a reproducible devcontainer!'));
app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Up on http://localhost:3000'));
```

- Quick start commands
```bash
# create repo skeleton
mkdir hello-devcontainer && cd hello-devcontainer && git init
mkdir -p .devcontainer
# add devcontainer.json, package.json, index.js (as above)
code .   # VS Code → Command Palette → Dev Containers: Reopen in Container
```

- Headless/CI equivalent
```bash
npx @devcontainers/cli up --workspace-folder .
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Repo + .devcontainer/devcontainer.json] --> B[VS Code: Reopen in Container]
  B --> C[Build image + install Features]
  C --> D[postCreateCommand: npm ci]
  D --> E[Ready: uniform env + ports forwarded]
  E --> F[Repeatable on any machine/CI]
```

- Key outcomes
  - Same tools and versions for everyone
  - One-click start; seconds to switch contexts
  - Config lives with code; easy to share and review

slides.narration:
Let’s build a working development environment from scratch and prove why devcontainers simplify your life... I’m starting with an empty folder, and in three minutes we’ll have a uniform, repeatable environment that anyone on the team can run.

I’ll create a new project folder, initialize Git, and open it in VS Code... Inside, I’ll add a .devcontainer folder with a single file, devcontainer.json... This file is our environment as code... I’m choosing the lightweight base image and adding the official Node Feature, pinned to version twenty so everyone gets the exact same runtime... I’m forwarding port three thousand for our app, and I’ve set postCreateCommand to run npm ci so dependencies install automatically the first time the container is created... I’m also recommending the ESLint extension so every contributor gets the same editor setup.

Next, I’ll add two tiny app files... A package.json with a start script, and an Express dependency, and an index.js that serves a hello message on port three thousand... Nothing fancy—just enough to show the workflow.

Here’s the magic... In VS Code, I run Reopen in Container... VS Code reads devcontainer.json, builds or pulls the image, installs the Node Feature, and then runs our postCreate step... When it finishes, the status bar shows we’re connected to a Dev Container... That means my shell, tools, and editor extensions are now running inside a clean, standardized environment, regardless of my host operating system.

Let’s run it... In the integrated terminal—in the container—I type npm start... The app boots, VS Code forwards port three thousand automatically, and I can open the browser to see Hello from a reproducible devcontainer... No local Node installation, no path issues, no version drift.

Why does this matter?... Because this exact setup lives with the code... Every teammate and every contributor uses the same container, with the same tool versions, on any machine... Switching context between repos becomes painless because each repo defines its environment... And if you want to run this in CI or a headless environment, the Dev Container CLI gives you the same result with a single command, so your development and automation are aligned.

In short: we declared the environment once, we got a working app immediately, and we eliminated the class of bugs that start with it works on my machine... This is how devcontainers save hours on onboarding and minutes on every context switch, while making your environments predictable and easy to share.

content.title: Best practices + where the time savings come from
content.markdown:
- Best practices that unlock speed:
  - Pin everything: base image tags and Feature versions to eliminate surprise drift.
  - Use Features first, keep images lean, and run as a non-root remoteUser.
  - Split lifecycle hooks: postCreate for one-time installs, postStart for per-run tasks.
  - Prebuild in CI/Codespaces to cache image layers and dependencies.
  - Compose for app + DB to standardize local integration tests.

- Example: fast, repeatable setup
```json
{
  "name": "Web + API",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu-22.04",
  "features": {
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1": { "version": "20" },
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/python:1": { "version": "3.11" }
  },
  "remoteUser": "vscode",
  "postCreateCommand": "npm ci && pip install -r requirements.txt",
  "postStartCommand": "npm run db:migrate",
  "forwardPorts": [3000],
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": {
      "extensions": ["dbaeumer.vscode-eslint", "ms-python.python"]
    }
  }
}
```

- Where the time savings come from
```mermaid
flowchart LR
A[Clone repo] --> B[Open in Dev Container]
B --> C{Prebuild available?}
C -- No --> D[Build image + install deps\n10–20 min first run]
C -- Yes --> E[Pull prebuilt image + cached deps\n<1–2 min]
D --> F[Ready to code]
E --> F
F --> G[Switch branch or repo]
G --> H[Rebuild only what's changed\n~1–3 min]
```

- Measurable impact
  - Onboarding: hours/days → minutes
  - Context switching: 30–60 min → ~2–5 min
  - Fewer env bugs: consistent toolchains reduce “works on my machine” time

slides.narration:
Let’s talk about best practices, and exactly where devcontainers save you time... The theme is simple: make the environment deterministic and do heavy work only once.

First, pin everything... Lock your base image and Feature versions so every laptop and your CI get the same toolchain... Next, prefer Features over custom scripts; they’re maintained and cross‑architecture, which reduces surprises on Apple Silicon versus x86... Always run as a non‑root remote user for better security and production parity.

Split your lifecycle hooks... Use postCreate for one‑time installs like npm ci or pip install, and postStart for tasks that should run every time, like database migrations... That alone prevents re‑installing dependencies on every container start.

The biggest time win comes from prebuilds... Build the image and cache dependencies in CI or Codespaces so your first open pulls a ready‑to‑go image instead of compiling everything locally... Pair that with docker‑compose to bring up your app plus a database consistently, so integration tests are reliable from day one.

In practice, this cuts onboarding from hours or even days down to minutes... Context switching between repos or branches drops from half an hour to just a couple of minutes, because only what changed rebuilds... And you’ll spend far less time on “works on my machine” bugs thanks to consistent versions baked into the devcontainer... That’s how best practices turn into measurable, everyday time savings.

content.title: Pitfalls and quick fixes
content.markdown:
- Common pitfalls and quick fixes
  - Slow first build/start
    - Fix: Prebuild images; pin base image and Feature versions; move heavy OS/tool installs into Dockerfile layers.
  - File I/O slowness on macOS/Windows
    - Fix: Use cached mounts; keep node_modules in a named volume; prefer WSL2 on Windows.
  - ARM/x86 mismatch
    - Fix: Choose multi-arch images/features; only set platform as a last resort.
  - Secrets committed by accident
    - Fix: Use .env (git-ignored) and IDE/platform secret stores; never bake secrets into images.
  - Drift between dev and CI
    - Fix: Validate/build with Dev Container CLI in CI; pin versions; run tests inside the container.

```yaml
docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace:cached          # faster bind mount
      - node_modules:/workspace/node_modules
    # Only if unavoidable (prefer multi-arch images first)
    platform: linux/amd64
volumes:
  node_modules:
```

```bash
# Validate in CI with Dev Container CLI
# (e.g., in GitHub Actions step)
devcontainer build --workspace-folder .
devcontainer up --workspace-folder .
devcontainer exec --workspace-folder . npm test
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Symptom] --> B{Slow build?}
  B -->|Yes| B1[Prebuilds + cache in Dockerfile/Features]
  A --> C{File I/O slow?}
  C -->|Yes| C1[:cached mounts + named volumes + WSL2]
  A --> D{ARM/x86 mismatch?}
  D -->|Yes| D1[Use multi-arch images; fallback platform]
  A --> E{Secrets risk?}
  E -->|Yes| E1[.env + secret stores; never commit]
  A --> F{Dev/CI drift?}
  F -->|Yes| F1[Dev Container CLI in CI; pin versions]
```

slides.narration: Let’s wrap with the most common pitfalls and the quick fixes... First, slow first build or startup... Prebuild your dev container image, pin your base image and Feature versions, and move heavy OS or tool installs into the Dockerfile to leverage layer caching... Second, file I O slowness on macOS or Windows... Use cached bind mounts, keep node modules in a named volume, and prefer WSL2 on Windows for better performance... Third, architecture mismatches between ARM and x86... Choose multi‑arch images and Features wherever possible, and only force the platform as a last resort... Fourth, secrets accidentally committed... Never bake secrets into images or devcontainer.json—use a git‑ignored dot env file and your IDE or platform secret store... Finally, environment drift between development and CI... Validate and run your tests inside the dev container in CI using the Dev Container CLI, and pin versions consistently... With these quick fixes, you keep environments uniform, reproducible, and fast to start.

content.title: Wrap-up: Key takeaways and next steps
content.markdown:
**Key takeaways**
- Devcontainers = development environment as code: uniform, repeatable, portable
- Fewer “works on my machine” issues; faster onboarding and context switches
- Scales from single-service to full-stack (compose) and aligns dev with CI
- Prebuilds and Features cut setup time and drift

**Next steps**
- Start minimal, then layer in Features, compose, and prebuilds
- Validate builds in CI with Dev Container CLI
- Standardize editor settings and extensions in devcontainer.json

**Starter devcontainer.json**
```json
{
  "name": "Node Dev",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu",
  "features": {
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1": { "version": "20" }
  },
  "postCreateCommand": "npm ci"
}
```

**Adoption flow**
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Repo] --> B[Add .devcontainer/devcontainer.json]
  B --> C[Reopen in Container]
  C --> D[Add Features and editor settings]
  D --> E[Compose for services]
  E --> F[Enable prebuilds]
  F --> G[Validate in CI with Dev Container CLI]
```

**Resources**
- Dev Container Spec: https://containers.dev
- Features catalog: https://github.com/devcontainers/features
- Dev Container CLI: https://github.com/devcontainers/cli
- Codespaces docs: https://docs.github.com/codespaces

slides.narration:
Alright, let’s wrap up... Devcontainers turn your development environment into code, so everyone uses the same, repeatable setup... That means fewer “works on my machine” surprises, faster onboarding for new teammates, and quicker context switches between projects... And because the setup lives in your repo, it scales from a single service to full-stack with databases, while staying consistent with CI.

If you do one thing today, add a .devcontainer folder with a minimal devcontainer.json, reopen in container, and run your tests... Next, layer in Features for your toolchains, move to a compose setup if you have dependencies, enable prebuilds to speed startup, and validate builds in CI with the Dev Container CLI.

Resources are in the chat: containers.dev, the Features catalog, the CLI, and Codespaces docs... Make your environment boring in the best possible way so you can spend your time shipping, not configuring... Thanks for joining, and I’m happy to take your questions.
